We report a compact single-channel CPL (SC-CPL) spectrometer that alternates left-and righthanded emission through a piezo-actuated pair of orthogonally aligned achromatic quarter-wave plates using a rapid CCD detector. This design minimises moving optics and eliminates the need for detector matching and pre-calibration. It can operate in various acquisition modes such as time gated acquisition mode for long-lived CPL emission and a quasi-continuous mode for short-lived CPL emission. Validation against a benchmark PEM-CPL system using a range of CPL emitters reproduced fine CPL resolution with high sensitivity, orders of magnitude faster. This blueprint SC-CPL reported herein paves the way towards the world's first complete compact chiroptical toolbox. This could lead to significant advancements with pivotal scientific and societal impact.

item.title: Multistate Potential Energy Surfaces from an Equivariant Core-Hamiltonian Correction to Semiempirical Configuration Interaction
item.description: Nonadiabatic dynamics needs several coupled potential energy surfaces at once. Fitting each state separately discards the electronic structure that couples them, whereas semiempirical configuration interaction in the style of the orthogonalization-corrected OMx methods obtains all states from one Hamiltonian and thereby keeps the topology of their intersections. We propose to build multistate surfaces by learning inside this Hamiltonian. An equivariant network predicts a geometry-dependent correction to the one-electron core Hamiltonian, the operator that already carries the orthogonalization corrections of OMx methods, while the two-electron integrals keep their NDDO form. Configuration interaction then yields all states, their gaps, and analytic forces from the corrected operator, and the whole model is trained end to end on reference state energies. For 1,3-cyclohexadiene with XMS-CASPT2 references, the correction lowers the three-state error of refitted ODM3 from 0.222 to 0.096 eV on held-out geometries and halves the error of every state and gap. Along a new nonadiabatic trajectory propagated on the corrected surfaces, it agrees with XMS-CASPT2 to 0.09 eV, compared with 0.46 eV for published ODM3.

item.title: Streamlining Lateral Flow Assay (LFA) Data Analysis: A MATLAB® Live Script for Integrated Batch Image Processing and Limit of Detection Determination
item.description: Manual quantitative lateral flow assay (LFA) analysis can span at least three software environments: image-analysis software such as ImageJ, spreadsheets such as Excel, and coding tools using MATLAB, Python or R. Repeatedly defining Test, Control and background regions of interest (ROIs) for individual strips, transferring measurements and performing separate statistical and calibration analyses makes data analysis for standard-curve experiments laborious and introduces opportunities for manual handling errors. We present a one-stop MATLAB Live Script framework for single-image and batch LFA image analysis and data analysis. For batch calibration, researchers supply a folder of cropped LFA images with concentration and replicate information encoded in filenames, select the analysis settings and click MATLAB’s Run button once. The automated workflow then extracts line signals, combines replicate measurements, generates the calibration curve and determines the limit of detection (LoD), without manual intermediate measurements or data transfers. The framework supports sandwich and competitive assays with colorimetric or fluorescent/chemiluminescent readouts for strips containing one Test and one Control line. Quantification uses baseline-corrected peak areas or peak prominences, with optional Test/Control normalization. Algorithm-defined measurement regions avoid the variability of manually redrawn ROIs, enabling reproducible image quantification when the same images and analysis settings are reanalyzed. Calibration options include four-parameter logistic, five-parameter logistic, Hill, Langmuir, linear and two-term exponential models, with two direction-aware, blank-based methods for LoD determination. Diagnostic visualizations, input validation and analysis checks help reduce signal-extraction and calculation errors and make remaining failures visible for easier rectification, while model coefficients and goodness-of-fit statistics support interpretation. By automating the intermediate steps within one analysis environment, this framework streamlines LFA quantification and reduces opportunities for errors arising from repeated manual measurements and data handling in laboratory research and assay development. This document provides a detailed user guide to use the two MATLAB Live Scripts – for single strip and batch analysis.

item.title: Surface Stability of Alloys and Intermetallics during Electrochemical CO Reduction
item.description: Alloy catalysts for electrochemical CO2 and CO reduction are often screened on idealized, bulk-truncated surfaces, yet adsorbates and the applied potential can change which surface is actually stable under reaction conditions. Here, we combine density functional theory with surface thermodynamics to test whether active sites identified from *CO and *H adsorption energies persist in atomically dispersed single-, dual-, and tri-atom alloys, substitutional alloys, and intermetallic compounds. Two-dimensional surface phase diagrams, spanning the electrode potential and the CO chemical potential, show that adsorbates can reshape both surface composition and termination. *CO keeps Pd at the surface of the Pd1Au single-atom alloy, while the stable termination of intermetallic compounds such as SnPd and GaNi depends strongly on the elemental chemical-potential reference. Depending on this reference, the *CO and *H adsorption energies shift by up to ∼1 eV, so a site that appears active on an idealized surface may not exist under reaction conditions. Adsorption-energy descriptors should therefore be evaluated on thermodynamically accessible surfaces, and predictions for intermetallic candidates are most robust when their predicted active surface is independent of the chemical-potential reference.

item.title: SmartReact: An Open-Source Python Package for Scalable Forward Synthesis Enumeration Built on Interpretable SMARTS Templates
item.description: Predicting which products can be made from a set of building blocks underpins library design, analogue generation, and synthesis-constrained generative modelling. Reaction templates encoded as SMARTS patterns are the standard tool for this forward synthesis enumeration task. However, existing approaches force a trade-off between chemical coverage, specificity, and the computational cost of applying large template sets at scale. We present SmartReact, an open-source Python library that resolves this trade-off through a template set built on SMARTS-RX, a hierarchical functional group ontology. SmartReact's templates are a combinatorial expansions over the functional group ontology of 406 patterns based on which functional groups interact in which reaction, so the library exposes only a few hundred distinct reactant-side patterns no matter how many templates it holds, and one classification per molecule resolves thousands of templates at once. Every prediction of SmartReact is traceable to a named reaction and an explicit set of functional group requirements, making results directly interpretable by chemists and straightforward to audit. New reaction types can be incorporated by specifying a SMARTS pattern and its functional group requirements, making the library easy to extend. A case study enumerating 536 001 unique products from 1 000 building blocks in 14.1 s demonstrates real-world utility at scale.Scientific Contribution: SmartReact contributes a large, expert-refined SMARTS reaction template library together with an open-source Python package designed to use it efficiently. The library's 9 770 templates spanning 37 medicinal chemistry reaction types are generated by combinatorial expansion over the SMARTS-RX functional group ontology, which gives them a chemical specificity and non-redundancy that auto-extracted libraries lack and, at the same time, a bounded reactant-side pattern space that makes them cheap to pre-filter.

item.title: Novel Class of Small Molecules that inhibits Yellow Fever Virus replication
item.description: Yellow fever virus (YFV) is a mosquito-borne virus that causes an acute viral hemorrhagic disease in humans. The high morbidity, recurring large-scale outbreaks, vaccine shortages, and the absence of approved antiviral drugs continue to make YFV a major global health concern. Therefore, the development of safe and effective antiviral agents against YFV remains an urgent priority. In this study, we used a para-menthane monoterpenoid diol and various aldehydes to synthesize a broad series of heterocyclic compounds with hexahydro-2H-chromene and hexahydro-2H-4,6-(epoxymethane)chromene moieties. Evaluation of the antiviral activity of the synthesized compounds identified compound 8k bearing a the hexahydro-2H-4,6-(epoxymethano)chromene core as a potent novel inhibitor of YFV replication in vitro. Compound 8k significantly reduced extracellular viral RNA copies and infectious viral load, highlighting its potential as a promising lead for the development of novel anti-YFV therapeutics.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Networks Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling end-to-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. For a feed-forward neural network (FNN) using extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs), embedding the EoS reduces the average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 8.67% to 5.57%. Replacing the FNN and ECFP representation with a graph neural network (GNN) using cyclic polymer graphs further reduces the average MAPE to 2.58%. Pre-training the models on PC-SAFT parameters for small molecules, followed by fine-tuning on polymer PVT data, yields additional improvements, reducing the average MAPE to 5.06% for the FNN and 2.15% for the GNN. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining an embedded EoS with geometric deep learning, and transfer learning for accurate polymer PVT predictions.

item.title: Structure Responsiveness of fluorinated PEGylated Au Nanoparticles in Physiological Serum.
item.description: Understanding nanoparticle (NP) - protein interactions is critical for controlling colloidal behaviour in biological environments. Here, we study how the introduction of fluorinated moieties into the PEGylated shell of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) influences interparticle assembly and interactions with protein. Combining microfluidic diffusional sizing (MDS) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), we revealed that exposing fluorinated hydrophobic groups does not compromise the stealth properties of PEG ligands. Remarkably, no lasting protein corona forms in biological media or fetal bovine serum (FBS), as evidenced by unchanged hydrodynamic sizes. Instead, SAXS revealed alterations in shell scattering length density, thickness, hydration, and interparticle interactions—effects that depend on the hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic ratio in the shell. These structural reorganizations suggest a transient protein layer with fast exchange kinetics that modifies interparticle forces without stable protein adsorption, offering crucial insights for designing advanced nanomedicines.

item.title: Organocatalytic hydroboration of allenes promoted by boron-based ionic liquid
item.description: The first protocol for the organocatalytic hydroboration of internal allenes affording Z-alkenylboronates is reported. Efficient and selective addition of HBpin to 1-aryl-3-methylallenes proceeds at room temperature and under solvent-free conditions in the presence of boron-based ionic liquid, 2-butyl-3-ethyl-3-methyl-1,3,2-oxazaborolidinium methanesulfonate, [BEMBox][OMs]. The reaction tolerates various functional groups on the aryl ring and exhibits high regio- and stereoselectivity. These features make the developed protocol a green alternative to the previously reported metal-based methods.

item.title: Tyrosinase-Like Monooxygenation Activity of Mono- and Dinuclear, Surface-Depositable Cu(I) Pyridinophane Complexes
item.description: Dome-shaped, surface-depositable organometallic complexes are a novel approach for the heterogenization of catalysts. In this context, we synthesized three copper complexes which are supported by different mono- and dinucleating pyridinophane ligands (thiacalixpyridine TCPy, dithiapyridinophane PyPS and thiacalixpyridazine TCPdz). Their monooxygenase activities towards monophenolic substrates were investigated and the influence of cavity size and nuclearity was assessed. While the mononuclear TCPy and PyPS complexes are almost inactive, the dinuclear TCPdz complex exhibits a high reactivity. Furthermore, monolayers of a TCPdz based dicopper(I) thiocyanate complex were deposited on Au(111) and investigated with the help of surface spectroscopy (IRRAS, XPS and NEXAFS) demonstrating the formation of a chemically intact monolayer.

item.title: How Effective is DFTB for Investigating Electrochemical Interfaces? A Study of Metal-Water Systems
item.description: Density-functional tight binding (DFTB) has recently emerged as a computationally efficient alternative to density functional theory (DFT) for modelling metal-water interfaces. However, electrochemical interfaces are inherently grand-canonical, and it remains unclear whether DFTB can reliably capture potential-dependent electronic response beyond equilibrium properties. Here, we systematically benchmark standard self-consistent-charge DFTB for Au(111) and many-body ChIMES-DFTB for Pt(111) against grand-canonical DFT. Using H2O, OH, and H adsorbates in vacuum and under explicit solvation, we compare two charge-control strategies available in DFTB+: an electronic-constraint counter-electrode approach and a fixed-total-charge scheme. Adsorption energies, Fermi-level response, charge partitioning, and interfacial forces are evaluated across charged interfaces. The electronic-constraint approach reproduces the potential-dependent variation of the Fermi level more faithfully than the fixed-charge scheme, whereas both approaches yield similar adsorption energies and charge partitioning on fixed geometries. We further show that adsorption energetics depend more strongly on the underlying Slater-Koster parameterization than on the addition of many-body ChIMES corrections. Explicit solvation remains the principal limitation, amplifying errors in electronic response and interfacial properties. These findings identify key priorities for developing transferable DFTB models for realistic grand-canonical electrochemical simulations.

item.title: Mooney Viscosity from Steady-Shear Measurements in a Rubber Process Analyzer
item.description: The Mooney viscosity ML(1+4) is still the most widely used flow parameter of unvulcanized rubbers, although it is a torque and not a viscosity. This work derives the relation between the Mooney torque and the steady-shear viscosity. An analytical solution for the rotor faces and the annular gap, corrected numerically for the corners, gives a conversion factor U(n), which depends only weakly on the flow index n. At a representative shear rate of about 1.2 s−1, the Mooney viscosity is, therefore, proportional to the viscosity. The relation was checked against steady-shear flow curves measured in a rubber process analyzer (RPA) on filled compounds, EPDM raw polymers and natural rubbers. On average, the measured Mooney viscosity is 1.23 times the calculated one, with a scatter of about 8 %. Thirteen industrial compounds from a second laboratory confirm this empirical factor without adjustment. With ML ≈ 0.90 η(1.2 s−1)/(kPa s), the Mooney viscosity is predicted within the reproducibility of the Mooney test. The cause of the factor remains open; elastic effects at the edge of the rotor are a possible explanation. A closed-cavity rheometer which is able to measure in steady rotation, and not only in oscillation, can thus provide the Mooney viscosity for quality control in addition to cure kinetics and flow curves, which are needed for the description of processes such as injection molding, compression molding and extrusion.

item.title: Flash Communication: PhI(OTf)2 Exists After All.
item.description: We report the observation of the parent PhI(OTf)2. This compound had been incorrectly invoked in many reports, but has never been observed before. Based on work on related systems decomposition pathways for PhI(OTf)2 arising from reaction with TMS-F to generate PhI followed by nucleophilic attack of PhI onto PhI(OTf)2 to generate iodonium cations were identified. This mode of decomposition is mitigated simply by working at lower concentrations, allowing for generation of relatively clean solutions of genuine PhI(OTf)2. It is shown however that this parent oxidant may not be useful as any oxidative process resulting in PhI generation will trigger decomposition by iodonium formation as a competing reaction.

item.title: Direct observation of valence tautomerism in sublimated molecular sub-monolayers
item.description: This study reports the first observation of a sub-monolayer molecular deposit prepared by sublimation on a conductive substrate of valence tautomerism (VT), an entropy-driven rearrangement of valence electrons between a metal ion and an organic ligand in redox-labile coordination compounds. To this end, a neutral cobalt(II) complex including two iminosemiquinonate redox-active ligands was thermally sublimated under UHV conditions onto highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG). Scanning tunnel microscopy and UV photoelectron spectroscopy, flanked by DFT calculations, were used to investigate the morphology and occurrence of tautomeric equilibria at the monolayer level. Temperature-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) experiments provided evidence of the intactness of the molecular deposit and reversible VT behavior, which is characterized by an incipient, reversible transition at T > 300 K. Finally, the quantitative estimation of the phenomenon was achieved using soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), which allowed the determination of the effect of surface deposition on the thermodynamics of the VT process. These findings establish the feasibility of preserving reversible valence tautomerism in surface-supported molecular layers and highlight the potential of VT compounds as active components in hybrid molecular spintronic architectures.

item.title: 60-Second NIR Regeneration of H-Phase Nb2O5 from Production Scrap: A Sustainable, Scalable Route to High-Capacity Anode Recovery
item.description: The escalating demand for high-performance lithium-ion batteries has intensified the need for sustainable electrode material recovery strategies that minimise energy consumption and processing time. Here, we report a rapid, energy-efficient nearinfrared (NIR) irradiation approach for the regeneration of niobium pentoxide (Nb2O5) from production scrap comprising a slurry of Nb2O5 active material, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder and carbon black conductive additive. NIR irradiation at 100% intensity achieves simultaneous and complete decomposition of both binder and carbon black within 60 seconds, as visually confirmed by a colour transition from dark grey to white, a result that conventional furnace sintering achieves only after 8 hours at 600 °C, representing a reduction of more than two orders of magnitude in processing time. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) confirms the disappearance of the crystallisation and melting transitions associated with the binder phase following both treatments. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) demonstrate that NIR irradiation preserves the crystal structure and morphology of the regenerated Nb2O5 to a degree comparable with conventional thermal treatment. Raman spectroscopy confirms the complete elimination of the carbon black D and G bands in the treated materials, validating conductive additive removal. Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) measurements show that the regenerated Nb2O5 anode delivers a specific capacity of 232.58 mA h g−1, comparable with the furnace-treated material and consistent with the high-capacity H-Nb2O5 polymorph. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) confirms redox peak positions consistent with H-phase Nb2O5, while kinetic analysis reveals a hybrid charge-storage mechanism dominated by solid-state diffusion with a minor capacitive contribution, underpinning the high capacity and electrochemical stability observed. These results establish NIR irradiation as a time- and energy-efficient platform for closed-loop Nb2O5 electrode regeneration, with strong prospects for industrial-scale battery recycling.

item.title: On-the-fly Neural Network based Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations of NH3-SCR over Cu-CHA
item.description: Copper exchanged chabazite (Cu-CHA) is the preferred choice for abatement of NOx from lean burn engines. The low-temperature activity depends critically on the presence of paired [Cu(NH3)2]2 + complexes, which are required for O2 adsorption. The pairing of [Cu(NH3)2]2 + complexes has so far been studied by ab initio molecular dynamics or more recently molecular dynamics using machine learning force-fields. An alternative to molecular dynamics is kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) simulations, which enable simulations over longer time scales. In this study, an on-the-fly kMC model is developed where the rates for [Cu(NH3)2]2 + diffusion are evaluated on the fly using a machine learning force field (ML-FF). We find that the fraction of paired complexes depends sensitively on the zeolite composition and the aluminum distribution. The results reveal a large distribution of Cu pair stabilities and that only few Cu ions are paired, demonstrating the heterogeneous nature of Cu-CHA. A mean field model based on the fraction of paired complexes is used to explore how changes in zeolite composition affect the catalytic activity. The methodology of combining kMC and ML-FF to account for dynamic changes in catalyst structure during reaction conditions is general and provide a possibility to go beyond the often used static approximation when evaluating reaction rates.

item.title: Chemoselective Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling of NHC–Aryl Boranes in the Presence of Boronic Esters: Sequential One-Pot Synthesis of Unsymmetrical Terphenyls from Aryl-Linked Diboron Compounds
item.description: N-Heterocyclic carbene (NHC)–aryl boranes (Ar–BH2–NHC) were found to undergo direct Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling (SMC) with aryl bromides under Pd2(dba)3/XPhos catalysis, with no activation step. The reaction tolerated a range of aryl bromides, including one bearing a C–Cl bond that was left untouched. In intermolecular competition with an aryl pinacol boronate (ArBpin), the use of K2CO3 as a base in toluene–H2O delivered the NHC–borane-derived biaryl with 99:1 chemoselectivity. Extension to aryl-linked diboron compounds bearing both NHC–BH2 and boronic ester moieties revealed that selectivity depends strongly on the diol ligand: the Bpin derivative gave mainly the double-coupling product, whereas the sterically hindered BEpin (3,3,4,4-tetraethylethylene glycolato) derivative reacted with 99:1 selectivity at the NHC–borane site. Sequential addition of a second aryl bromide, K3PO4, water, and toluene to the same vessel enabled the one-pot synthesis of an unsymmetrical terphenyl in good yield.

item.title: CIPER: Interpretable Permeability Predictions Guide Cyclic Peptide Editing
item.description: Permeability optimization of synthetic cyclic peptides requires deciding which edits to pursue and 2 when to retain the parent. Each new analogue requires synthesis and permeability measurement, yet 3 a predicted improvement alone leaves the supporting chemical evidence unclear. We ask whether 4 explicit structural comparisons can support useful edit rankings and make their measured analogue 5 evidence traceable. We introduce CIPER, short for Context-Integrated Potential Edit Regression, which 6 learns assay-matched permeability differences and decomposes each prediction into exact contributions 7 from training molecules. Its primary model combines atomic chemistry with cyclic-residue context 8 through a fixed product kernel. A retrospective comparison of 16 fixed-ranking and sampling methods 9 covers 286 parent pools containing 4,213 measured candidate pairs. CIPER gives the highest mean 10 gain among the 11 methods sharing the permitted training labels at all three query budgets under 11 equal chemical-component weights. One CIPER query recovers 0.518 log10 units of improvement, 12 exceeding 0.491 from four random queries; four queries reduce random-selection regret by 75.1%. Its 13 leading gains at the first two budgets persist under parent-equal and source-equal weighting. Separate 14 tests on 1,213 complete panels assess when to retain the parent, while signed contributions identify 15 measured analogues supporting or opposing each recommendation. CIPER thus connects effective 16 edit prioritization and parent retention to inspectable structural evidence, providing specific analogue 17 comparisons for prospective synthesis and permeability measurement. 18 Scientific Contribution. CIPER links edit ranking and parent retention to measured structural analogues within one property-difference model. Its exact signed decomposition exposes the evidence behind each recommendation, while common-pool comparisons demonstrate early enrichment of improving candidates. This connection turns a predicted permeability change into a chemically inspectable decision and identifies analogue relationships for prospective testing.

item.title: Automated Construction of Data-Efficient Machine-Learned Force Fields for Polymers
item.description: General-purpose machine-learned force fields (GP-MLFFs) provide near-first-principles accuracy across broad chemical spaces, but their reliability is limited by training coverage and reference level of quantum mechanics. We present an automated active-learning workflow using the open-source package aims-PAX that builds on GP-MLFF sampling to generate targeted, higher-accuracy reference data for fine-tuning or training models with task-specific architectures. We demonstrate this approach by training a single model on approximately 4,000 hybrid-DFT structures spanning seven chemically distinct polymers. The model predicts densities and glass-transition temperatures with accuracy comparable to GP-MLFFs trained on hundreds to thousands of times more data, supports stable molecular dynamics of approximately 10,000 atoms, and transfers to unseen polymers. An explicit dispersion term is indispensable in this low-data regime, providing the inter-chain cohesion that GP-MLFFs must otherwise learn implicitly from large datasets. Replay fine-tuning extends the model to silicon-containing polydimethylsiloxane while preserving accuracy on the original polymers. Beyond collective properties, the aims-PAX model better describes the local response to hydrogen bonding. The model reproduces experimentally observed frequency shifts of the nylon-6 amide group, which a polymer-specific GP-MLFF captures only partially, and their cooperative enhancement along hydrogen-bonded chains, which a classical force field cannot represent. These results establish aims-PAX as a data-efficient route from general-purpose sampling to specialized MLFFs, combining targeted chemical coverage, suitable architectures, and the reference accuracy the problem requires.

item.title: Site-Dependent Promotion of CO Hydrogenation on Rh(211): Role of Impurity Stability and Step-Edge Charge Distribution
item.description: First-principles calculations were used to investigate direct CO hydrogenation along the step-edge of the Rh(211) surface, modified by substitutional 3d transition metal impurities (X = Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu) occupying either the step-edge or the terrace lattice site. Impurities at the step-edge site substantially lower the activation barrier relative to pristine Rh(211), with Ti inducing the lowest energy barrier of 0.80 eV, followed by Cr, V, and Mn. The enhanced promotion associated with the step-edge impurities correlates with a dipole-like charge distribution between neighboring step-edge atoms. Results revealed that while Ti, V, and Cr are highly active at the step-edge site, these metals segregate to the terrace site, whereas Mn and Fe are nearly thermoneutral between step-edge and terrace sites and can still provide a reduction of CO hydrogenation barriers. MnMn and FeFe models, with same element impurities co-substituted at both step-edge and terrace lattice sites, further reduce the energy barriers to 0.95 and 1.00 eV, respectively, relative to their corresponding single-impurity models. These demonstrate that effective promotion of CO hydrogenation on Rh(211) requires direct step-edge site participation, thermodynamic accessibility of the active impurity configuration, and local charge polarization at the active sites.

item.title: The Same Edit, a Different Outcome: Relational Learning for Cyclic Peptide Permeability
item.description: The same local modification can enhance cyclic-peptide permeability in one chemical background 2 and reduce it in another. Molecular difference learning predicts property changes from structure 3 pairs; the question here is what the relationships between an edited residue and its surroundings 4 add to that prediction. We introduce an edit-relational Gaussian process that encodes the residue 5 relationships gained and lost through a graph-certified modification, retaining stereochemistry and 6 native connectivity. In retrospective replay of 286 parent pools and 4,213 measured parent–product 7 pairs, relational inputs improve two-measurement gain over a matched descriptor Gaussian process 8 in all five chemical components. Their component-weighted mean gain is 0.588 log10 permeability 9 units, versus 0.537 for an ExtraTrees descriptor ranker at the same budget and 0.491 for four random 10 measurements. Controls with a shared first mean-ranked choice locate the principal measured benefit in 11 the representation and initial ranking. Measured stereochemical reversals across methylation backgrounds 12 motivate prospective tests of whether solvent-dependent amide exposure predicts where edit benefits 13 transfer. Changed residue relationships thus supply predictive distinctions that help a model recognize 14 when the chemical background changes the value of an edit. 15 Scientific contribution. We extend molecular difference learning with the residue relationships 16 changed by a certified local edit. Matched Gaussian-process comparisons show that these inputs add 17 predictive value beyond parent physicochemical descriptors and their changes. Measured interaction 18 panels identify the background dependence that this representation seeks to capture, while finite-pool 19 analysis separates candidate resolution from measurement allocation. 20

item.title: Sunlight-Driven Photo-Reductive Mineralisation
item.description: Perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are highly persistent molecules whose widespread use and global distribution have created an urgent need to develop effective remediation strategies. Here, we address this research gap by exploiting zinc sulfide (ZnS) for the photo-reductive mineralisation of PFASs under natural sunlight and ambient conditions. We found sulfur vacancies (Vs) within the ZnS lattice, produced during supercritical synthesis, to be responsible for visible-light absorption and enhanced photocatalytic activity. Complete mineralisation of PFOS was achieved in both batch (3 mL) and continuous circulating flow (12 mL) after 24 h of ultra-violet (UV-A, 365 nm) irradiation. Analysis of transformation products and scavenger studies revealed that C–F bond cleavage was driven by direct photoelectron reduction. The treatment of various PFASs and field-derived aqueous film- forming foam (AFFF) contaminated water revealed chain length and head group dependent activity associated with compound adsorption and reduction potential (from density functional theory calculations). Ultimately, the demonstrated natural sunlight activity (under ambient temperature and pressure) highlights the potential of supercritical ZnS as a scalable, sunlight-active PFAS remediation technology.

item.title: Deciphering Metal-Ion Effects in Engineered Ethylene-Forming Enzymes through Electronic and Electrostatic Reactivity Descriptors
item.description: The selective activation of strong aliphatic C–H bonds remains a fundamental challenge in catalysis due to their high bond dissociation energies and limited chemical differentiation. In biological systems, nonheme FeIV=O intermediates serve as powerful oxidants, enabling challenging C–H transformations such as L-arginine oxidation in ethylene-forming enzymes (EFEs). Here, we investigate how metal substitution modulates the structure, electronic configuration, and reactivity of the EFE active site by replacing iron with manganese and cobalt. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that all three metals maintain stable coordination within the protein matrix, while revealing a conserved hydrogen-bonding network that generates strong, oriented local electric fields along the M=O axis. Quantitative LEF analysis identifies Arg171 as a dominant electrostatic contributor that elongates the M=O bond and stabilizes high-spin configurations across all variants. Hybrid QM/MM calculations uncover pronounced metaldependent differences in C–H activation barriers, with CoIV=O exhibiting the lowest barrier, followed by MnIV=O and FeIV=O. Multireference CASSCF computations reveal that these trends originate from symmetry-breaking orbital bifurcation within the M=O unit, leading to variable degrees of oxyl radical (M–O•) character. Importantly, C–H activation proceeds via a protein-enforced π-channel hydrogen-atom transfer mechanism in all cases, independent of metal identity or formal spin state. Together, these results establish oxyl radical character, regulated by protein electrostatics and metal-dependent electronic flexibility, as the primary determinant of reactivity in EFE-like systems, offering general design principles for biomimetic high-valent metal–oxo catalysts.

item.title: The RMSD ceiling: an information limit on geometry-based transition-state metrics
item.description: Machine-learning models for transition-state (TS) geometry prediction are almost universally benchmarked by the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, or by the mean absolute error of the interatomic-distance matrix (D-MAE), relative to a reference TS. We show that these Euclidean measures are unreliable proxies for the quantity a practitioner actually needs: whether a predicted geometry optimizes to a genuine TS at a target level of density functional theory. We optimized 520 interpolation-based guesses for 260 reactions from the Transition1x database [Schreiner M., Sci. Data 2022, 9, 779] at the r2SCAN-3c level. Every geometry-based quality measure–Kabsch-aligned RMSD, D-MAE, a reaction-coordinate projection, and cheap semi-empirical descriptors–saturates in a narrow band of the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC), 0.77–0.84, for predicting optimization success, and 18% of guesses within 0.28 Å of the reference fail nonetheless.

item.title: On-Demand CO2 Transport via Magnetically Programmed Orientation of Metal–Organic Framework Crystals in Mixed-Matrix Membranes
item.description: Mixed-matrix membranes (MMMs) offer an energy-efficient alternative to thermally driven industrial separations and a direct route to lower carbon emissions. In metal–organic framework (MOF)-based MMMs, crystallographic orientation can influence molecular transport, yet its contribution is difficult to isolate from other microstructural factors. Here, we exploit the intrinsic magnetic anisotropy of Dy5L6(OH)3 (L = 3-amino-4-hydroxybenzoate) crystals to control crystallographic orientation within a 6FDA-DAM matrix without magnetic additives. Casting without a magnetic field favored an in-plane c-axis orientation, whereas magnetic-field-assisted casting produced an out-of-plane orientation, in agreement with the calculated magnetic susceptibility anisotropy. The out-of-plane membrane showed over 70% higher CO2 permeability than the in-plane membrane at comparable CO2/N2 selectivity in singleand mixed-gas permeation tests. This enhancement arose primarily from increased diffusivity, consistent with a substantially lower calculated CO2 migration barrier along the c axis than within the ab plane. Crystallographic orientation thus emerges as a design parameter for MOF-based MMMs.

item.title: Dynamic interplay between water and surface carbonates mediates oxygen exchange kinetics in oxide catalysts
item.description: Decorating oxide catalysts with basic oxides decreases surface acidity and lowers the work function, which facilitates electron donation to adsorbed reaction intermediates and thereby enhances oxygen exchange kinetics. However, facilitating electron transfer also renders acid-base-engineered catalysts prone to deactivation by interplay with acidic gas species. The present study investigates the effects of H2O and CO2 on the oxygen exchange kinetics of Ca-decorated SrTi0.65Fe0.35O3‑δ. Both surface hydroxylation and surface carbonate formation diminish the oxygen exchange kinetics relative to measurements conducted without intentionally added gas phase impurities, consistent with increased surface acidity and a higher work function of the catalyst. However, when surface carbonates are present before H2O exposure, water mediates carbonate decomposition, resulting in an apparent improvement in oxygen exchange kinetics relative to the initial catalyst state. This water-mediated decomposition of surface carbonates proceeds at substantially lower temperatures (T~300°C) than thermal carbonate decomposition in dry oxygen. Our findings help reconcile conflicting reports on the beneficial and detrimental effects of water on oxygen exchange by linking them to the surface acid-base properties and resulting electronic structure of oxide catalysts.

item.title: Phase Resetting of the Pinned Pair of Spirals through Transient Chaotic Dynamics in a Chemical Reaction-Diffusion System
item.description: Excitable chemical reaction-diffusion systems show complex spatiotemporal nonlinear dynamical behaviors. Utilizing the ferroin-catalyzed BZ medium, we characterized the collective dynamics of spiral waves through experimental imaging and numerical simulations with a modified Oregonator model. Here, in this article, we report the emergence of self-regulatory behavior in a Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) medium, where the spirals are pinned to spherical heterogeneity, lose initial phase synchronization on imposition of a perturbation through a mild concentration gradient imposed internally with cation exchange resin beads, which further recovers to achieve an adaptive lag synchronized state through the transient chaotic dynamics. This is loosely analogous to the homeostasis-like behavior. This work advances the mechanistic understanding of nonlinear chemical dynamics and explores the competition between the internal gradient and coupling strength to build an adaptive intelligent system that can be applied to designing chemically driven self-healing systems, error correction in unconventional computing, and many other disciplines.

item.title: nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT: Spin-complete mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT with a noncollinear exchange–correlation kernel
item.description: We present nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT, a spin-complete mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT with a complete noncollinear exchange–correlation response. The theory unifies the two extensions of MRSF-TDDFT, the noncollinear kernel of nc-MRSF and the spin-complete closed–virtual (CV) space of CV-MRSF, in a single response operator. Three parameter-free rules supply every density-functional interaction that the completed CV space requires: the transverse kernel is added wherever exact exchange acts, the Coulomb interaction of a singlet-coupled CV pair is completed with its longitudinal kernel, and the semilocal spin potential enters one-electron elements as its spin average. As a result, the response yields spin-pure states, is covariant under separate closed, singly occupied, and virtual orbital rotations, and recovers the isolated Tamm–Dancoff excitation matrices of a closed-shell fragment separated from the reference open shells, which triplet-pair degeneracy alone does not ensure. With 20–25% exact exchange, nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT gives lower Thiel singlet and triplet errors than either parent method. At this common optimum of nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT and conventional TDDFT for singlet excitations, the singlet excitation energies of the two methods are comparable, while the B1LYP singlet–triplet gap MAEs on Thiel and QUEST are 71–77% lower with nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT than with conventional TDDFT in the RPA or TDA. However, the principal advantage of the method lies beyond vertical excitations: as a spin-complete mixed-reference response that treats ground and excited states on an equal footing, it is expected to carry this accuracy into strongly correlated regimes where single-reference TDDFT fails, including diradicals, bond breaking, doubly excited states, and conical intersections.

item.title: External Force-free Unpinning and Wave-Break of Pinned Spirals in a Chemical Reaction-Diffusion System
item.description: Excitable media demonstrate patterns; the spiral is one of them. These spiral patterns are also present in the human cardiac system, where they can get pinned in the presence of spatial heterogeneities. Here, we investigate the response of pinned spiral waves in a Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction to an internally generated and temporally evolving chemical heterogeneity, in the form of a gradient produced by Amberlite IR-120 ion-exchange resin beads. The resin establishes a mild concentration gradient and modifies the medium’s local chemical environment, producing spatial changes in ion concentrations and altering local excitability. Under these conditions, pinned spiral tips slowly detach from the glass-bead obstacles without the application of an external electric or thermal field. We observed unpinning and wave fragmentation near the resin line. The unpinning occurred at the tip closer to the resin in all our experiments with 10 and 12 resin beads, whereas nearly 36.4% of the experiments with 8 beads showed the first unpinning away from the resin line. These results indicate that the evolution of chemical heterogeneity and local excitability can jointly regulate the stability of pinned spiral waves. The work provides a physicochemical framework for studying unpinning of spiral waves under a mild gradient and with evolving heterogeneity in excitable media; it will be relevant to biological excitable systems, including cardiac tissue.

item.title: Automated Mapping and Parameterization of Coarse-Grained Force Fields for Dissipative Particle Dynamics
item.description: We present a procedure for the automated mapping and parameterization of coarse-grained (CG) models for dissipative particle dynamics simulations. In our mapping methodology, a given molecule is represented as a graph, and its CG representation consists of a renormalized graph in which groups of vertices (representing heavy atoms) are contracted to single vertices (representing CG particles). Our mapping algorithm identifies functional groups in the molecule and leverages efficient graph-theory-based algorithms to find an optimal mapping for a given mapping scale. This mapping is subject to the constraint that certain functional groups remain intact within the resulting CG particles. To parameterize the corresponding CG force field, we apply an iterative Boltzmann inversion-like procedure to determine parameters for the bond, angle and nonbond potentials. This is accomplished by fitting valence geometries, and the integral of the pair distribution functions for the CG model to an all-atom reference simulation. We validate our approach by automatically calculating octanol-water partition coefficients for a dataset consisting of 454 simple organic compounds. Comparing these to experimental values results in a correlation coefficient of 0.92, indicating the robustness of our coarse-graining procedure in producing viable CG models. In addition, we demonstrate the utility of the procedure on a drug formulation involving a nano emulsion reproducing the size of the globules observed in experiment.

item.title: Bisnucleophilic Ambident Reactivity of Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes via Lewis Acid Catalyzed Aldol-Ene Cascade: Diastereoselective Synthesis of Fused Oxabicyclic Scaffolds
item.description: The substantial strain embedded within the compact framework of bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) has established them as versatile 1,3-dipolar synthons for strain-release transformations. However, these advances have exclusively relied on the ambiphilic reactivity of BCBs. In contrast, their ambident reaction modality has remained unexplored, despite its potential to fundamentally expand the reactivity landscape of BCBs and provide access to previously inaccessible chemical space. Herein, we report the first bisnucleophilic reaction of BCBs via a Sc(OTf)3-catalyzed annulative coupling with succinaldehyde, enabling direct access to cyclobutene-fused oxabicycloheptanes in high yields with complete diastereocontrol. Distinct from the conventional 1,3-functionalization of BCBs, this transformation features formal 1,2-functionalization and reveals a previously unrecognized aldolene-type reactivity of this highly strained scaffold. This cascade protocol is operationally simple, scalable, and broadly tolerant of functional groups, while the resulting products provide streamlined access to densely functionalized fused cis-[2]-ladderane and angularly fused isoxazolidine scaffolds in diastereomerically pure form.

item.title: Mechanistic Understanding of Proton Transport in Metal–Organic Frameworks via Universal Machine-Learned Potentials
item.description: Proton transport in porous materials is an integral process in science and engineering. Recently, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as promising nanoporous materials for proton-exchange membranes (PEMs); however, the fundamental understanding of proton transport in MOFs remains unelucidated. Here, we developed universal machinelearned potentials (uMLPs) to investigate proton transport properties and mechanisms in pertinent MOFs, namely UiO-66 and MOF-808. After validating the prediction accuracy across diverse physical properties, we fine-tuned a uMLP to simulate proton transport in bulk water and MOFs. Importantly, the uMLP accurately reproduced the experimental proton diffusivity in bulk water, which cannot be achieved via conventional potentials. Subsequently, uMLP-driven molecular dynamics (MLP-MD) simulations reveal that proton hopping (Grotthuss mechanism) is governed by hydrogen-bond (H-bond) structure. Our mechanistic analysis reveals previously unelucidated insights into the proton transfer mechanism: MOFs with smaller pores exhibit higher energy barriers for proton transfer and H-bond exchange, thereby inhibiting proton hopping under nanoconfinement. Furthermore, the effects of incorporating linker-functionalization and defects in MOFs were investigated; while linker-functionalization exacerbates nanoconfinement and hinders proton transfer, incorporating defects facilitates proton hopping by lowering energy barriers for proton transfer and H-bond exchange. Finally, analysis of structure-transport relationships evidences that H-bond structure governs proton transport in MOFs. Beyond developing accurate uMLPs for describing complex proton transport across diverse MOFs, we reveal previously unexplored mechanisms of proton transport under nanoconfinement and elucidate key structure−transport relationships that will guide the design of PEMs.

item.title: alchemy: bounded enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks
item.description: Automated construction of chemical reaction networks is limited by the combinatorial growth of possible molecules, intermediates, and formal transformations. We present alchemy, an open-source Python workflow for systematic enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks. Within an explicitly bounded graph space, alchemy generates connected, neutral C/N/H molecular graphs with single, double, or triple bonds and specified radical counts; RDKit sanitisation and canonicalisation then remove graph-invalid and duplicate records. Formal reaction candidates are constructed without learned reaction templates by combining bond-dissociation records into rearrangement and transfer stoichiometries. Parallel generation, persistent disk-backed storage, and Kuzu graph representation make the resulting formal network searchable. An independent brute-force control recovers exactly the same 416 neutral molecular graphs as alchemy in a three-heavy-atom C/N/H space. In a trimethylamine case study limited to at most five heavy atoms and one unpaired electron per reaction side, the workflow generated 41,735 unique molecular graphs and a seed-0 bounded sample of 60,035 first-generation reaction records. The reaction construction is not complete because high-frequency shared fragments are handled by a documented deterministic sampling cap. An optional PaiNN molecular-energy model is distributed with the software, but its closed-shell QM9 benchmark does not validate the open-shell species considered here and its output is not used to rank, filter, or interpret the case-study records. alchemy therefore provides a reproducible route to bounded reaction-space construction and downstream graph inspection.

item.title: Synthesis and Electronic Properties of Pentafluorosulfanyldifluoromethyl-Substituted Alkynes
item.description: Pentafluorosulfanyldifluoromethyl-substituted alkynes are synthesized from terminal aryl alkynes and SF5CF2I under 370 nm LED irradiation, providing access to the SF5CF2–C≡C–Ar framework. For phenylacetylene, irradiation at 450 nm favors the vinyl iodide SF5CF2–CH=C(I)–Ph. Comparative calculations reveal connectivity-dependent charge distributions in the alkyne unit. Natural population analysis indicates smaller carbon–carbon charge differences for the CF2-linked architecture than for directly sulfur-substituted analogues, whereas Mulliken analysis gives the opposite trend.

item.title: MALDI-MS for Fast Analysis of PFOS Partitioning in Bacterial Biomass
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants whose interactions with biological matrices are increasingly important to characterize. Conventional PFAS analysis in biological matrices using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) methods typically require extensive sample extraction and cleanup, limiting the throughput of PFAS screening. In this work, we developed a matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS) workflow for direct detection and quantification of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) in bacterial biomass following exposure. Bacteria are ubiquitous in natural and engineered environments and may contribute to PFAS fate and transport. The diversity of PFAS structures and bacterial species leads to many exposure scenarios, making it an ideal system to develop fast screening methods for PFAS partitioning. Calibration curves of different ranges were first evaluated in both water and Escherichia coli (E. coli) biomass matrix-matched samples. Stable isotope-labeled internal standard, 13C8-PFOS, was used for both calibration curves and samples to enable quantification. E. coli suspensions were exposed to PFOS, and the resulting biomass was washed, added with internal standard, lysed, and directly deposited onto a MALDI target with 1,5-diaminonaphthalene as the MALDI matrix for analysis. Comparable, low-ppb (µg/L) limit of quantification was determined for calibration curves in water and biomass sample matrices. Using external calibration curves and isotopically labeled standards, we quantified the amount of PFOS associated with bacterial biomass and found that the partitioning is time- and dose-dependent. The workflow allowed direct detection of PFOS from processed bacterial biomass with significantly reduced sample preparation and instrumental analysis time, establishing MALDI-MS as a rapid and quantitative approach for PFAS analysis and providing a foundation for higher-throughput screening of PFAS across diverse biological samples.

item.title: Highly β-Selective Synthesis of 2-Deoxy N- and C-Glycosides via Photoredox/Cobalt Catalysis: Total Synthesis of Streptcytosine G
item.description: Herein, we report an independently developed photoredox/cobalt-catalyzed radical–polar crossover strategy for the highly β-selective synthesis of 2-deoxy N- and C-glycosides directly from readily available glycals. The synthetic utility of this approach is demonstrated through late-stage glycosylation of bioactive molecules and its application to the total synthesis of streptcytosine G. These findings expand the synthetic applicability of photoredox/cobalt-catalyzed glycosylation to complex carbohydrate substrates and natural product synthesis.

item.title: DFT/XCIS: A Kohn-Sham Approach to Extended Configuration-Interaction Singles, for Valence- and Core-Level Spectroscopy of Open-Shell Systems
item.description: Core-to-valence transitions are sensitive probes of unoccupied valence orbitals and are especially informative for open-shell molecules and materials, where frontier molecular orbitals are often degenerate or nearly so. Accurate simulation of core-level spectra for open-shell molecules is challenging because methods such as time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) typically rely on a spin-unrestricted reference determinant, leading to spin contamination. A restricted open-shell reference state eliminates spin contamination in the ground state but excited states computed using the configuration-interaction singles (CIS) approach may yet exhibit significant spin contamination. This can be eliminated by extending the CIS excitation space to include a small number of doubly substituted determinants, in what has been called “extended” (X)CIS, and this approach affords a variational and size-consistent wave function for each excited state, free of spin contamination but also free of dynamical correlation. Here, we introduce the latter via density functional theory (DFT), using Kohn-Sham orbitals within the XCIS formalism and scaling the electron repulsion integrals to reduce double-counting of correlation effects. Reasonable valence excitation energies are obtained with the new DFT/XCIS approach, and combing it with core/valence separation (DFT/ XCIS-CVS) extends the method to core-level spectroscopy. Absolute excitation energies for K-edge transitions are improved, relative to conventional TDDFT, by means of an empirical shift in the 1s eigenvalues. Incorporation of dynamical correlation improves the accuracy of spectral splittings for open-shell systems, relative to the recently reported XCIS-CVS approach.

item.title: Multimodal LLM-Assisted Diagnosis of Cryptic Failure Modes in High-Throughput Experimentation: A Case Study in Gold Nanorod Synthesis
item.description: Self-driving labs typically optimize experiments within a predefined design space. Yet high-throughput campaigns can fail for reasons outside this design space, including reagent state, stock solution quality, and handling history. Here, we present a case study of a five-plate high-throughput gold nanorod synthesis campaign in which a multimodal large language model (LLM) helped diagnose such cryptic failure modes. We used low-cost camera images for rapid assessment of seed and synthesis state, with UV-vis spectroscopy when the images were insufficient for interpreting experimental outcomes. The campaign included an abnormal seed batch, a plate-wide failed synthesis in which most wells showed weak spectra with a strong rise toward the near-infrared, and a visually plausible synthesis with an apparent spectral discontinuity subsequently attributed largely to plasmon mode switching. Instead of responding to failed synthesis by further optimizing the screened concentrations of silver nitrate and ascorbic acid, the LLM intervened by questioning the upstream factors, including seed preparation and reagent handling, helping researchers investigate causes outside the combinatorial design space. To compare spectral consistency across runs, we defined a UV-vis spectral roughness metric based on local spectral interpolation across the synthesis grid. The final synthesis had the lowest roughness, Rspec=0.636 compared with ~0.772 for earlier successful runs, and the highest median longitudinal-window absorbance. Our results show the potential of multimodal LLMs upstream of autonomous optimization in self-driving labs to identify when an experiment has failed for reasons outside the nominal design space and when additional characterization is needed before optimization should continue.

item.title: Minimum Knowledge Collaboration enables joint materials development through protected optimization
item.description: Materials companies must jointly develop products that meet competing requirements while keeping their formulations, processes and models private. Sample exchange alone can leave their searches poorly coordinated. We introduce Minimum Knowledge Collaboration (MKC), which connects private Bayesian optimizers through bounded candidate descriptions and company-specific search directions. Mathematical analysis links representation error, feasible private responses and information-limited search. In 256 controlled synthetic programs, all methods pursued the same reachable product target, defined as 100%. After 64 complete-product tests, MKC reached 92.4%, the information-rich reference 93.8%, and reusable better, neutral or worse feedback 6.0%. By 2,048 tests, ternary feedback reached MKC's result in 30 of 32 simplest bilateral programs; attainment across all 1,024-candidate programs was 12.5%. A cross-study scenario calculation gave a 0.0063% complete-state reconstruction index. This assumption-based design screen complements the measured reconstruction results. MKC demonstrates coordinated product development with bounded disclosure and supports industrial evaluation.

item.title: Hydrophilic Silica Surfaces Host a Hydrophobic-Like Two-Dimensional Water Network
item.description: Silica–water interfaces are widely considered prototypically hydrophilic due to surface silanol groups enabling hydrogen bonding with interfacial water. However, this description primarily accounts for vertical surface–water interactions and neglects possible collective in-plane/horizontal organization of interfacial water. Using DFT-MD combined with graph theory, we show that water at crystalline and amorphous SiO2 surfaces systematically forms a highly collective two-dimensional hydrogen-bonded network within the Binding Interfacial Layer (BIL). This extended lateral network is a structural feature typically associated with hydrophobic interfaces, yet it coexists with heterogeneous vertical hydrogenbonding motifs involving surface silanols that anchor the network without disrupting its connectivity. These results demonstrate that silica wettability cannot be reduced to surface–water interactions alone, but emerges from the interplay between vertical anchoring and lateral water–water hydrogen-bond organization, suggesting a revised molecular framework for oxide–water interfaces. This might represent a paradigm shift in the molecular-level description of wettability at hydrophilic oxide interfaces.

item.title: CFD Evaluation of a Tesla-Type Micromixer for Chemical Processing
item.description: Tesla-type micromixers mix well in published studies but are rarely used in industrial flow reactors. This study evaluates whether the modified Tesla micromixer of Hong et al. could be used for continuous chemical processing by considering mixing together with pressure drop, throughput and flow structure. A 3D model with eight Tesla units (channel 200 µm wide, 110 µm deep) was simulated in SimScale as a transient laminar water flow at Re = 10, 50 and 70, and mixing was tracked with a passive scalar. At Re = 10 the streams mixed gradually along the whole mixer; at Re = 50 and 70 they were fully mixed after about two units. From Re = 10 to 70, however, the flow rate increased 7 times while the pressure drop increased 29 times (2.7 to 78 kPa), one mixer processed at most 80 mL/h, and low-velocity regions formed inside the bends. A four-unit mixer still mixed fully at Re = 50 and 70 with about half the pressure drop, but its throughput and blocking risk were unchanged. The Tesla micromixer is therefore limited not by mixing but by throughput, pressure drop and possible blockage, which explains why it is used in lab-on-a-chip devices rather than in production.

item.title: Bioisosteric Design of Novel Flavonoid-Derived Aromatase Inhibitors to Reduce Estradiol Biosynthesis in ER+ Breast Cancer
item.description: ​​Estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer is a hormonal cancer in which tumor proliferation is dependent on estrogen via androgen-to-estrogen conversion, facilitated by the aromatase enzyme (CYP19A1). Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are often first-line treatments for ER+ breast cancer, yet the three FDA-approved agents present potentially mitigable pharmacological issues and distinct side-effect profiles. To expand structural diversity and improve pharmacological properties, a computational hit-to-lead pipeline was executed. A virtual hit screen of ten selected natural flavonoids against human aromatase (PDB ID: 3S79) across 100 dockings revealed Chrysin consistently outperformed other flavonoid ligands on all measured thermodynamic metrics, with 51% of poses scoring an energy (ΔG) ≤ -5.9 kcal/mol. Using target-based and bioisosteric substitution, a lead series of Chrysin-based analogs called Arcflavonoids (ARC) were engineered in PyMOL. SwissADME predicted the ARC series was lead-like and potentially features reduced cross-inhibition of the major drug-processing CYP450 enzymes, relative to existing commercial AIs. Utilizing comparative molecular docking, we observed that all ARC ligands demonstrated steroidal cleft coordination and no heme-iron interaction. Through steroidal cleft interaction, a top lead, ARC48, achieved a predicted best pose featuring a ΔG < -10.00 kcal/mol and an inhibition constant (Ki) of 10.34 nM. However, only ARC45 and ARC46 appear to have consistently competitive thermodynamic metrics with testosterone while potentially outcompeting androstenedione.​

item.title: Experimental redox tuning of designed ferredoxins through sulfur to selenium substitutions
item.description: Iron–sulfur (Fe–S) clusters are essential for electron transfer in biology, and their redox potentials are finely tuned by both first-sphere ligation and the surrounding peptide environment. Here, we investigate both how minimal peptide scaffolds control cluster redox properties and how chalcogen substitution modulates these effects. Two designed peptides, corresponding to 28 residues of a bacterial ferredoxin-like sequence were assembled with both [4Fe–4S] and [4Fe–4Se] clusters, allowing a direct comparison of sulfur-to-selenium substitution within identical scaffolds. UV–visible and EPR spectroscopy were consistent with cluster incorporation and predominantly dimeric assemblies. Voltammetry measurements showed redox energetics were dependent on both chalcogen identity in a cubane cluster, and on the peptide environment. Minimal motifs capture sequence-dependent environmental effects on cluster redox chemistry and highlight the potential of chalcogen substitution combined with peptide design for bioinspired tuning of electron-transfer properties.

item.title: When Can a Molecular-Dynamics Simulation Stop?
item.description: Molecular-dynamics (MD) simulations are usually run for a prespecified duration, even when the goal is to estimate an equilibrium observable to a stated precision. Stopping as soon as an estimated uncertainty becomes small enough is attractive, but repeated inspection invalidates uncertainty statements calibrated for a fixed time. We formulate data-dependent stopping as an inferential problem with an explicit precision target and a simultaneous-in-time coverage requirement, and organise it into four gated stages: temporal prediction against strong baselines, uncertainty calibration, an anytime-valid stopping rule, and measured high-performancecomputing (HPC) savings. We report exploratory first-stage results on four incrementally assembled ATLAS cohorts, using sequence-grouped cross-validation and a target computed only from frames after a 20 ns prefix. In the largest cohort (757 systems, 1,243 replicas, 689 sequence groups), ridge regression on 48 prefix summaries and a residual gated recurrent unit (GRU) both reduced RMSD mean absolute error relative to last-value persistence (0.610 and 0.636 versus 0.673 Å; paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero), whereas the GRU–ridge difference was not significant in any cohort. A genuine structure-only baseline, a compatible mdCATH analysis, sequential coverage and HPC cost measurements are still outstanding, so no stopping policy or computational saving is claimed.

item.title: eRoboChem: Autonomous Electrosynthesis Across Redox Modes and Reactor Designs
item.description: Synthetic electrochemistry offers powerful opportunities for molecular synthesis, yet its broader adoption remains hindered by the complexity of electrochemical reaction development. Beyond conventional reaction parameters, electrosynthesis requires careful choice of electrode materials, reactor designs and control of electron transfer, creating a complex experimental and optimisation challenge that can deter many synthetic chemists. Here, we introduce eRoboChem, a modular self-driving laboratory that integrates automated experimentation, analytical feedback and Bayesian optimisation across complementary flow and batch electrochemical reactors. Its versatility is demonstrated through three transformations spanning paired, oxidative and reductive electrosynthesis, each presenting distinct experimental challenges. Fully closed-loop flow operation enables autonomous reaction optimisation while accommodating gas evolution, whereas a complementary human-in-the-loop high-throughput batch module addresses electrode passivation and facilitates electrode screening. Systematic comparisons with conventional optimisation strategies, including one-factor-at-a-time and design of experiments approaches, demonstrate the value of Bayesian optimisation for navigating complex reaction spaces and extracting chemically meaningful and complementary insights. By adapting the experimental architecture to the requirements of the chemistry, rather than constraining the chemistry to a fixed reactor design, eRoboChem establishes a flexible framework for autonomous electrosynthesis and represents a step towards making electrochemical methodologies more accessible to the broader synthetic community.

item.title: Automated flow microscale synthesis of gamma-modified PNA unveils structural determinants of RNA hybridization
item.description: Peptide nucleic acids (PNA) are synthetic nucleic acid mimics in which the negatively charged sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA and RNA is replaced by a neutral pseudopeptide backbone. This neutral backbone reduces dependence on ionic strength, provides resistance to protease and nuclease degradation, and promotes high-affinity binding to complementary nucleic acids. Modification at the γ-carbon of the backbone can further improve solubility, reduce aggregation, and preorganize the backbone into a chiral helical conformation. However, the steric demands of γ-modified PNA (γPNA) monomers, together with on-resin aggregation and base-mediated side reactions, make γPNA difficult to synthesize efficiently. Here, we report an automated flow microscale synthesis (AFMS) platform for rapid preparation of N-(2-aminoethyl)glycine PNA (aegPNA), L-serine γPNA (LS-γPNA), and hybrid PNA (hPNA). Independent control of coupling and deprotection temperatures enabled rapid amide-bond formation in 10 s while limiting base-mediated degradation and provided access to long PNA sequences with high fidelity and high purity. Preparative strong cation-exchange chromatography further isolated target PNA from side products unresolved by reverse-phase high performance-liquid chromatography. This synthesis-to-function workflow enabled evaluation of how LS-γPNA content and distribution influence RNA recognition. Unexpectedly, increasing γPNA incorporation enhanced duplex thermal stability while progressively reducing intracellular splice-correction activity, revealing that productive RNA targeting requires a balance between backbone preorganization, conformational adaptability, and target-engagement kinetics.

item.title: Development of an Anionic Multicomponent Reaction for Rapid Construction of Highly Functionalized Dearomatized Scaffolds
item.description: Biosynthetic dearomatization of 3,5-dimethyl orsellinic acid (DMOA) affords highly functionalized cyclohexadienone precursors for enzymatic polyene cyclization to produce numerous complex meroterpenoids. In particular, dearomatized scaffolds derived from 2,4-dihydroxyl-3,5-dimethylphathalide (DHDMP) are valuable synthons for synthetic access to meroterpenoids. Driven by a practical need to obtain scalable amounts of the requisite dearomatized motifs, herein we report an anionic, multicomponent reaction sequence for construction of such scaffolds from ester, Michael acceptor, and acyl chloride reaction partners. The reaction entails sequential Michael-Addition of an ester enolate, Acylation, and Dieckmann Annulation (MADA). The utility of the method is demonstrated through several examples and downstream derivatizations, including the synthesis of farnesyl-DHDMP, a key biosynthetic precursor to meroterpenoids.

item.title: Direct C(sp3)–H/C(sp2)–F Cross-Coupling of Methylpyridines with Aryl Fluorides
item.description: Direct C(sp3)–H functionalization of methylpyridines is intrinsically challenging. Herein, we report a transition-metal-free, silylboronate-mediated heterobenzylation of methylpyridines with aryl fluorides. The combination of a silylboronate and KOtBu enables direct C(sp3)–H/C(sp2)–F coupling under mild conditions, providing efficient access to structurally diverse azaarylmethanes. The reaction accommodates π-extended aryl fluorides, polyfluoroarenes, and various 4-alkylpyridines, including substrates bearing multiple potentially reactive C–H or C–F bonds, with useful levels of chemo- and regioselectivity. The method is also applicable to the late-stage functionalization of structurally complex molecules. Alkyl fluorides are also compatible via the C(sp3)–H/C(sp3)–F coupling reaction. Mechanistic studies, including aryl-halide comparison, radical-trapping, investigation of pronucleophile, Hammett plot, competition experiments, and DFT calculation support an ionic pathway involving generation of a heterobenzylic nucleophile followed by nucleophilic substitution of the C–F bond. For electronically neutral and electron-rich aryl fluorides, the observed reactivity is consistent with a concerted SNAr pathway. This strategy provides a complementary approach to conventional transition-metal-catalyzed heterobenzylic arylation and expands the synthetic utility of organofluorine compounds as coupling partners for C–C bond formation.

item.title: Comparative Assessment of Degradation Pathways for Enzymatic Degradation of Polybutylene Terephthalate (PBT) and Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) and their Degradation Intermediates
item.description: Elucidating how polymer chemistry and substrate crystallinity collectively determine polyester degradability is a key to advancing enzymatic recycling as it enables predictive assessment of the degradation behavior of novel substrates and accelerates the development of efficient recycling strategies. Achieving this requires a systematic comparison across different polymer chemistries and crystallinity states. However, direct comparative studies remain scarce. Here, we compare the enzymatic degradation pathways of amorphous and semicrystalline poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) and poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT) using the cutinase LCCiccg. Degradation pathways are characterized through changes in soluble degradation products, surface chemistry and morphology, surface and bulk crystallinity, semicrystalline structures, and mechanical properties. Identified degradation intermediates are synthesized and evaluated for their enzymatic and abiotic hydrolyzability and inhibitory effects on polymer degradation. Across both polymers, enzymatic hydrolysis follows the same cleavage mechanism, whereas substrate crystallinity determines the extent to which degradation can proceed and thereby governs the resulting morphological and mechanical changes. The findings further support a common desorption–readsorption mechanism linking chain accessibility to localized hydrolysis and the persistence of crystalline domains. Collectively, these results reveal two independent axes of transferability: the enzymatic cleavage mechanism is conserved across polymer chemistries, whereas the resulting morphological and mechanical responses are governed primarily by substrate crystallinity.

item.title: How Ready Are Universal Machine-learned Interatomic Potentials for Carbon Capture Simulations?
item.description: Nanoporous materials offer a tunable platform for selective carbon capture through adsorption, and identifying the best candidates requires computational screening built on accurate and transferable models of host–guest interactions. Classical force fields (FFs) have enabled rapid large-scale screening but fail to accurately describe such interactions for challenging systems, and while universal Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials (u-MLIPs) promise to bridge this gap, their ability to predict macroscopic adsorption observables across chemically diverse frameworks remains largely underexplored. Here we benchmark 25 u-MLIPs against experimental CO2 adsorption data for nine metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) spanning rigid open-pore, open-metal-site, and confined small-pore classes, and find that quantitative isotherm prediction remains out of reach for the evaluated general-purpose models. We show that failures trace to two distinct error sources, the MOF–CO2 and the CO2–CO2 interactions, whose relative contribution shifts with framework chemistry, so that isotherm accuracy cannot be inferred from any single energy metric. In rigid open-pore and confined small-pore MOFs, the MOF–CO2 error dominates, while in strongly interacting frameworks with open metal site (OMS) both MOF–CO2 and CO2–CO2 descriptions become controlling factors, and error cancellation between the two sources can produce simulated accurate isotherms for physically incorrect reasons. Dataset composition, rather than architecture alone, determines whether a model reaches quantitative accuracy, and models trained on explicit MOF–CO2 and multi-molecule CO2 configurations perform most consistently. The evaluation protocol introduced here separates the two error sources and defines concrete paths for advancing u-MLIPs toward reliable computational screening for carbon capture.

item.title: Hessian- and Property-Aware Learning of Analytic Bond-Order Potentials
Gradient ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE)–a primer on quality functions and pulse shape penalties
item.description: Quantum optimal control is a versatile, powerful method to tailor quantum experiments. In NMR, numerical quantum optimal control algorithms such as the gradient ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE) algorithm have sparked many developments in pulse shaping, pushing the limits of pulse selectivity and robustness. To provide an overview of its core principles and the many expansions it has undergone ever since its introduction, the most common quality functions are benchmarked in their ability to guide the spin state transfer for facilitating excitation, inversion, and maximum quantum coherence. Explicit derivations of gradient and Hessian formulas are given, both summarizing what is known from the literature and complementing it. The derivations also give due consideration to the fact that spin states can be represented as density operators or spin operators. Analogously, the most common penalties to guide optimization toward experimentally feasible controls are discussed along with their explicit gradient and Hessian formula derivations. The discussion is complemented by thorough benchmarking for the most commonly used optimization algorithms.

item.title: A Transferable Deprotonated Tyrosine Residue for Amber and CHARMM Force Fields
item.description: The deprotonated form of tyrosine gates proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) in ribonucleotide reductase and photosystem II, forms the anionic chromophore of fluorescent proteins, and acts as a general acid/base in enzymes, yet a validated, transferable tyrosinate residue for routine fixed-charge protein simulations in the major Amber and CHARMM force fields is lacking. Here, we construct a deprotonated tyrosine residue (TYM) by transferring quinoid phenolate valence parameters, QM-validated for the fluorescent protein chromophore, and phenoxide parameters to standard Amber14/19/99SB* and CHARMM36m force fields. We validate the deprotonated residue against ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of a tyrosine side chain analog in water and experimental protein tyrosine pKa values. The best-performing force fields attain an AUE of roughly 0.5 pK units across 17 residues and preserve the catalytic Tyr57–Tyr16 hydrogen bond in ketosteroid isomerase.
